ANNY YU Shenzhen YM Clothing… • 11K followers When TSMC Rewrites Priority: Not About Apple But About Who Shapes the Next 10 Years of Silicon For years, Apple was seen as the untouchable VIP inside TSMC. Priority capacity. Early access. Structural privilege. That era is quietly ending. Surface-level facts are easy to list: • TSMC raised prices on Apple • Long-standing priority shipment protections were reduced • NVIDIA overtook Apple in certain quarters as TSMC’s top customer But none of these explain the real shift. The real question is simpler and more uncomfortable: Who determines TSMC’s capacity allocation, capital spending, and technology roadmap for the next 5–10 years? That is where power lives. In the past, Apple was the perfect customer: • Predictable, massive annual volumes • First mover for new nodes • Risk absorber for TSMC’s capex cycles But in the AI era, stability is no longer the scarcest resource. Explosive scalability is. NVIDIA’s orders are different: • A single product line can absorb enormous wafer volume • GPU + CoWoS + HBM form system-level demand • Growth within one generation is exponential, not linear For TSMC, this means higher capacity density and far greater margin elasticity per customer. Apple SoCs: • Highly customized, but limited die size • Packaging complexity is controlled • Margins sit mainly at the system level (iPhone, Mac) NVIDIA AI chips: • Reticle-scale die • Advanced nodes + advanced packaging • One order drives wafers, packaging, testing, materials NVIDIA is not buying wafers but buying TSMC’s future capacity structure. Apple designs for efficiency, yield and cost stability. NVIDIA designs to: • Push physical limits • Expose process bottlenecks • Force ecosystem upgrades From TSMC’s perspective, boundary-pushers are not just customers. They are co-developers of future nodes. Why C.C. Wei is rumored to personally engaged Apple? No single customer will retain permanent structural privilege. Price increases and priority removal happened together Because this wasn’t a negotiation, it was a redefinition of the customer hierarchy. Apple is not weaker. But it is no longer the industry’s central variable. Long-term implications are clear: • Early-node exclusivity will be harder to sustain • Chip cost pressure will structurally rise • Compute narratives have shifted from devices to data centers The semiconductor industry has shifted from consumer-electronics-driven to compute-infrastructure-driven. Apple is a capacity user NVIDIA is a capacity shaper TSMC has no choice but to follow physics, not history. Apple didn’t lose VIP status. It lost the default center position of the previous era. NVIDIA leads, but concentration risk is real. The future is about who defines physical limits and shapes capital efficiency. In every industrial cycle, power doesn’t disappear. It relocates. The harder question is: when power moves from brands to infrastructure, which business models stop making sense even if revenues still look fine? #SemiVon #AIInfrastructure 3

Market chatter suggests AMD is working with Google on v10 technology, per DIGITIMES Asia. Neither company has confirmed anything. The scope remains unclear. What is not unclear: Broadcom signed a Supply Assurance Agreement in April to develop and supply future TPU generations through 2031. MediaTek continues handling SerDes and I/O dies for inference variants. Those relationships are locked in. So where does AMD fit? The speculation centers on CPU cores, not compute dies. Sources familiar with the matter point to hybrid designs for reinforcement learning workloads — models that need on-package CPU integration alongside specialized accelerators. That is where AMD's experience with advanced packaging and CPU IP becomes relevant. This is not AMD replacing Broadcom. It is Google adding another tool. Broadcom still brings networking expertise and training-focused compute. MediaTek still brings cost efficiency on inference I/O. AMD potentially brings CPU cores that can sit on the same package and handle workloads that do not map cleanly to pure tensor operations. Multiple foundries. Multiple design partners. Modular architectures that let you swap in the best available component for each function without redesigning the entire system. NVIDIA built its dominance on vertical integration. The hyperscalers are building theirs on strategic disaggregation. Carol Lee Jointchips Technology Co., Ltd • 5K followers SK Hynix has officially completed production validation of its 375-layer 3D NAND (V10), confirming plans to start mass production by late 2026 at its M15 fab in Cheongju. Originally targeted as a “400-layer-class” device, the stack was adjusted to 375 layers due to extreme manufacturing complexity at higher counts. The core innovation is molybdenum (Mo) replacing tungsten (W) in word lines—the first full-scale adoption of Mo in high-stack NAND. As layers shrink, tungsten’s resistance spikes, slowing signals and requiring extra barrier layers that waste vertical space. Molybdenum cuts resistance by 30–50%, enables direct deposition without barriers, and boosts density—critical for 480/604-layer roadmaps. SK Hynix will retrofit existing lines (176/238/321-layer) instead of building new fabs, lowering costs. With AI/SSD demand booming, this Mo-based 375-layer NAND will deliver faster read/write, higher yield, and lower per-bit costs—strengthening SK’s position against Samsung and Kioxia. #SKHynix #3DNAND #SemiconductorTech #MemoryInnovation 1

Duke Huang USEMI LIMITED • 233 followers SiTime Bolsters Timing Portfolio with Renesas-Acquired Clocks The two companies are also partnering to integrate a MEMS resonator with an MCU in a single package. Source: EE Times In a landmark $3.2 billion deal, precision timing specialist SiTime is acquiring Renesas' timing assets, consolidating its position as a pure-play market leader. This move allows SiTime to expand from MEMS oscillators into Renesas' clocking portfolio, aiming to dominate the high-growth AI and data center timing markets. Strategic Moves for Both Players SiTime’s Play: Captures Renesas’ 30-year legacy clock portfolio (generators, buffers, synchronizers), instantly boosting its clocking revenue by >10x and adding 10,000+ customers. Post-acquisition, >60% of SiTime’s revenue will come from AI data centers and communications. Renesas’ Shift: Sharpens focus on embedded processors while entering a strategic collaboration to integrate SiTime’s timing tech into its MCUs—a move toward balance sheet discipline after a decade of acquisitions. Market Impact & Financials The acquired assets, expected to close by end of 2026, will add ~$300M in first-year revenue, nearly doubling SiTime’s current sales. Renesas’ timing business derives ~75% of revenue from AI/cloud and communication sectors—aligning perfectly with SiTime’s growth trajectory. A New Frontier: Integrated Timing SiTime’s MEMS resonators will be combined with Renesas’ MCU/SoC dies in a single package. Eliminates external timing components, saving cost, space, and power for critical applications like AI servers, automotive ADAS, and wearables. Outcome: First MCUs requiring no external timing parts, though market availability will take 2–3 years for design and qualification. Broader Implications The deal positions SiTime as a full-spectrum timing supplier, while Renesas gains a board seat (CEO Hidetoshi Shibata) and access to SiTime’s advanced resonators. For the industry, it signals a shift toward highly integrated, power-efficient timing solutions for next-gen AI and edge applications.
